newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Hamas charities garner support in Gaza.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hamas charities garner support in Gaza.

text.p: When Safah was born three months ago, her mother left her to die in the sandy strip separating Gaza from Egypt.
"No one goes there. It was just by chance (she was found)," said Youssef Khaled Zahhar, director of the Mercy Society for Children.
Zahhar, with a thick beard and the faint black mark of a pious Moslem on his forehead, takes in Gaza's unwanted children. Safah is one of them.
His orphanage, housing 40 babies and toddlers, is part of a vast network of Islamist charities supported by Hamas.
The military wing of the fundamentalist group is believed to be behind a double suicide bombing that killed 13 people and the two bombers in a Jerusalem market on July 30.
Among Gaza's poor, Hamas is a welcome provider of food and $100 monthly pittances.

Its combination of secrecy, militancy and altruism has made Hamas violence hard to fight. Every time the authorities crack down on the group, they risk public outcry by hurting a network of charities that keeps thousands of Gazans dangling just above desperation.
"We are serving this society. We are giving (these children) what their fathers did not give them," said Zahhar, whose brother is a Hamas spokesman.
Zahhar spent 40 days in a Palestinian jail during a PLO crackdown on fundamentalists. Unable to find work after getting out, he accepted a post as the orphanage's director.
"We are preparing these children to understand the meaning of Islam. We can tell them to pray and teach them about Allah," he said.
ISRAEL SAYS HAMAS CHARITIES JUST A FRONT

Hamas inspires young men to strap bombs on their chests and blow themselves up in Israeli buses in attacks that have claimed dozens of lives since Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation signed an interim peace deal in 1993 which Hamas opposes.
"It's used as a front," said Israeli government spokesman Moshe Fogel, referring to Hamas's charity work.
"A suicide bomber is told before he goes out, 'You'll get hundreds of virgins in heaven and your family will be taken care of,'" he said.
Israel accuses Hamas of using its charities to recruit young suicide bombers. Hamas denies this.
"We do it for the sake of God only," said Hamas leader Ismail Abu Shanab. "But politically, it creates a beneficial by-product.
"If the families are satisfied economically and socially, they will send their sons to the mosque. The mosque will educate them and lead them in the path of Islam," he said.
"Later on will come the political ideology."
Eight refugee camps dot the impoverished Gaza Strip, where unemployment tops 26 percent, but jumps to more than 60 percent during Israeli closures imposed after suicide attacks.
An average Gazan worker supports a family of 10 on $11 to $28 a day.

Islamist charities have left virtually no part of Gaza untouched. They employ hundreds of workers, including drivers, kindergarten teachers and guards. Thousands of families send their children to Islamist youth camps in the summer and take them to Moslem clinics when they fall ill.

"My father brought me. He wanted me to learn from good people how to be educated, to have manners, to have morals and to learn computer," said 14-year-old Ahmad Hiriz, who is attending an Islamic Association summer boys' camp.
Behind him, other boys marched to the beat of a drum after finishing a game of soccer.
"Our constitution is the Koran," they shouted. "Death by martyrdom is the best wish."
"It is purer here. The air is clean. It is a better atmosphere than just playing in the streets with no aim," Hiriz said.
PAST PLO CRACKDOWN HIT CHARITIES HARD
Under pressure from Israel after a series of suicide bombings killed 57 people 17 months ago, the Palestinian Authority cracked down hard on Hamas charities.
They detained more than 900 Hamas and Islamic Jihad activists, seized computer disks and files, and raided schools and mosques to undermine Hamas.
"At that time they tried to destroy everything," Zahhar said.
"They took some computers and some files from the orphans. Some people feared to work in associations like this because we will be under suspicion."
Israel also cracked down, closing Gaza's borders and refusing entry permits to thousands of Palestinian workers.
Palestinian analysts say the measures weakened Hamas, which had slowly begun to recuperate when the latest bombs hit.
Israeli leaders accused the Palestinian Authority of not being tough enough against "terrorism" and called for strident steps against Moslem militants.

Two years ago, Hamas distributed monthly salaries to about 6,000 Gazan families. About two-thirds of the recipients were families of political detainees and "martyrs" killed by Israel. The rest were simply poor, Abu Shanab said.
Now, only 2,000 to 3,000 families get funds.
"We have many poor families, and we cannot reach them, and the situation has deteriorated," Abu Shanab said. "But we know that Islam will rise again to correct the whole bad situation."
He said the poor would realise the Palestinian Authority was against them.
"These (poor) people will support Hamas, because people who were getting money from Hamas, and who now find Hamas has no money, they will say, 'Who prevented us from getting our money?'" he said.
Zahhar said the charities won't be shut down. He pledged to build family-style flats for his orphans once they outgrow their cribs and mats.
"You know, we call this social work," he said. "No one can stop it."
